title: Three questions to ask to find out if its really love
author: Jonny Thomson
summary: Thomson opens by admitting that decades inside the Greek to Roman to European tradition have left him ignorant of everything outside it, an ignorance he likens to owning a house and living in only one lit room. An interview with the Tibetan Buddhist master Tulku Lobsang Rinpoche supplies the unlocked door, and the piece turns on Rinpoche's distinction between attachment and love. Attachment clings, possesses, and grows jealous; love is presented instead as a set of three antidotes to the poisons that make us suffer. Kindness answers anger by reading other people's intentions charitably, illustrated with a shopper who turns to confront a stranger and finds an embarrassed child with a cart. Compassion answers attachment by granting room to change, since we tend to bind a partner to the version of them we first met or the version we keep in our heads. Bodhicitta answers ignorance by requiring that we see the world from the other person's position rather than assuming the limits of our own mind are the limits of the world. Thomson converts the three into diagnostic questions a reader can put to any relationship, and closes by defining love as finding your own joy in the joy of another.
points: The essay's organizing distinction is between attachment and love, with attachment treated as possessiveness and love as a set of three corrective practices.
Each element is framed as an antidote to a specific failure, kindness to anger, compassion to attachment, and bodhicitta to ignorance.
Thomson's compassion section makes the sharpest point, arguing that we bind partners to an earlier or idealized version of themselves and deny them room to change.
The three elements are turned into practical self examination questions about charitable reading, space, and perspective taking.
The piece doubles as an argument for reading outside one's own philosophical tradition, using the image of a house whose other rooms stay locked.
quotes: I've spent decades studying mostly the Greek to Roman to European to American philosophical tradition. Everything else is kind of an embarrassing darkness. It's like having a house and living only in one room.
Rinpoche argues that there is a difference between attachment and love. Attachment is when we cling to another person. We get possessive of them. We get jealous. We don't give them space.
Anger is often about perceived offense, and kindness is what sees people not as obstacles or as enemies, but as allies. Kindness softens the way we look at others' intentions.
Second, there is compassion. Compassion is the antidote to attachment, because attachment is what holds people too tightly. Attachment is what keeps the bird in the cage.

But compassion gives someone the room to change into somebody different from what we might have expected of them. Love allows the other to move forward on their own terms and not according to some rat's maze we've constructed for them.
Because it is ignorant to try to understand the world from only your point of view. It is ignorant to assume the limits of your mind are the limits of the world.

Bodhicitta accepts this and seeks to see things not only from another point of view but, in love, from another person's point of view. It tries to see the world with their eyes, to understand their needs, and to experience things from their position.
Because love is not about desperately clinging to somebody or seeking your own happiness in somebody else. It's when you find your own joy in the joy of another.
